Note on the staging script: `scripts/library-profile-check.mjs --staging` prints 18 'duplicate id / duplicate profile' lint lines for each file only because the installed copy of the same profile already exists in the library; there are no other lint problems. I ran an equivalent wrapper (kept outside the recheck folder, in a scratch subfolder) that ignores exactly those duplicate lines and runs the same lint plus the same one-question-per-facet retrieval check: all three files print OK (9 records each, every facet found). Retrieval is unaffected by my edits because only conv text changed (no name, topic, kw or parent), but note the retrieval check answers from the installed copy for the same ids.

corrected.was: barbed wire, patented in 1874, is a common symbol of the end of the open range.
corrected.now: barbed wire, in the form Joseph Glidden patented in 1874, is a common symbol of the end of the open range.
corrected.why: Barbed wire had earlier patents (Kelly 1868 and others); what Glidden patented in 1874 (in May, and the well-known No. 157,124 in November) was the design, the one that won in the courts and the market. The old wording implied barbed wire itself was first patented in 1874.

remainingDoubts: 'The first western' is genuinely contested (Wister is convention; Emma Ghent Curtis's The Administratrix, about 1889, is cited by some). Record stays contested and the watch note already says so.

softened.was: Alexandre Dumas's The Three Musketeers and The Count of Monte Cristo, both begun in 1844, added pace, swordplay and the serial instalment.
softened.now: Alexandre Dumas's The Three Musketeers and The Count of Monte Cristo, both begun as newspaper serials in 1844, added pace and swordplay.
softened.why: Both were begun as newspaper serials in 1844 (Le Siècle, Journal des Débats), which is confirmed; but Dumas did not 'add' the serial instalment, the newspaper roman-feuilleton already existed. The claim now says what is true and drops the invention credit.

softened.was: In the early twentieth century the pulp magazines carried adventure to mass audiences: Edgar Rice Burroughs's Tarzan (first printed in a magazine in 1912), Arthur Conan Doyle's The Lost World (1912), Rafael Sabatini's Captain Blood (1922) and the hero-magazine serials of the 1930s.
softened.now: In the early twentieth century magazines and popular novels carried adventure to mass audiences: (same list)
softened.why: The Lost World ran in the Strand Magazine (April to November 1912), which was a mass-market monthly, not a pulp; Captain Blood was a novel in 1922. Tarzan (All-Story, October 1912) is the pulp case. The lead-in no longer labels all of them pulps.

softened.was: The decades from the 1880s to the First World War were adventure's high point in Britain: ... Buchan's The Thirty-Nine Steps (1915)
softened.now: The decades from the 1880s into the First World War years were adventure's high point in Britain: ...
softened.why: The Thirty-Nine Steps (1915) was published during the war, so 'to the First World War' contradicted its own example.

remainingDoubts: 'The first adventure novel' is definition-dependent (Robinson Crusoe is the convention); the record is contested and the watch note says so.

corrected.where: profile-war-fiction-history, conv 3 (The Red Badge of Courage)
corrected.was: written by an author too young to have fought in it
corrected.now: written by an author born years after the war ended
corrected.why: Crane was born on 1 November 1871 and the Civil War ended in 1865, so he was not a young man who missed the fighting but was born after the war. Confirmed by search; the old wording misstated the situation.

corrected.was: written during the war and looking back at it, as in Parade's End and Birdsong.
corrected.now: written during the war and long after it, as in Under Fire, Parade's End and Birdsong.
corrected.why: The old sentence said the books were written during the war but gave two examples written in the 1920s and in 1993. Under Fire (1916) is the during-the-war example, and the rest are after.

softened.was: usually credited to Gertrude Stein and popularised by Hemingway, who used it as an epigraph to The Sun Also Rises (1926).
softened.now: it is popularly credited to Gertrude Stein, who said she took it from a Frenchman, and Hemingway used it as an epigraph to The Sun Also Rises (1926).
softened.why: Sources agree Stein did not coin it: Hemingway's memoir says she took it from a French garage owner, her own account names a hotelier, and Hemingway's epigraph is the reason it is famous. The new wording keeps the usual credit and states what is known. This now matches the library's own Lost Generation entry ('popularly credited').

remainingDoubts: 'First modern war novel' for The Red Badge is a critics' label; I found no source using that exact phrase. The text already presents it as 'often called' and the first-war-novel point is in the watch note as a convention, so it is left.
